note: Source files are Logos-exported plain-text excerpts of NTC vol. 12-13 (Hendriksen & Kistemaker, Baker, 1953-2001). Print page numbers are not preserved in the export, so 'page' is given as the Romans chapter:verse range on which Hendriksen comments. NTC volume 12 covers Rom 1-8; volume 13 covers Rom 9-16.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_for.page: Rom 8:29-30 / 9:11-13 (NTC vol. 12 ad loc.; cf. also Rom 9 chapter introduction)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_for.chapter: Chapter 9, Section 2: Divine Election and Rejection (9:6-18); cross-reference to comment on Rom 8:29-30 in vol. 12
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_for.quote_verbatim: Even the doctrine of divine predestination, for which one generally turns immediately to Rom. 9:10-24; 11:5-8, 29, is foreshadowed in 8:29, 30.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_for.context: Hendriksen explicitly identifies the 'golden chain' of Rom 8:29-30 (foreknowledge -> foreordination -> calling -> justification -> glorification) as the basic sequence of the divine decree, and locates its formal exposition in Romans 9-11. He repeats that 'In the final analysis the reason why some people are accepted and others rejected is that God so willed it. The divine, sovereign will is the source of both election and reprobation. Human responsibility is not canceled, but there is no such thing as human merit. God's eternal purpose is not ultimately based on human works' (comment on Rom 9:6-13).

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_pre.page: Rom 9:6-18 (comment + 'Additional Reflections on Election and Reprobation')
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_pre.chapter: Chapter 9, Section 2: Divine Election and Rejection
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_pre.quote_verbatim: What Paul is saying, then, in verses 6-13, is this: In the final analysis the reason why some people are accepted and others rejected is that God so willed it. The divine, sovereign will is the source of both election and reprobation. Human responsibility is not canceled, but there is no such thing as human merit. God's eternal purpose is not ultimately based on human works.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_divine_pre.context: Hendriksen treats Rom 9:6-13 as the locus classicus for double predestination. Cases of Jacob/Esau, Isaac/Ishmael, and Pharaoh illustrate that 'salvation, appropriated by faith, was definitely a matter of divine, sovereign grace. Human merit had nothing to do with it.' He then cites Westminster Confession III.I, V, VII as creedal confirmation of the same doctrine.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_potter_and.chapter: Chapter 9, Section 3: God's Wrath and Mercy (9:19-29)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_potter_and.quote_verbatim: The main idea Paul is putting across is this: If even a potter has the right out of the same lump or mass of clay to make one vessel for honor, and another for dishonor, then certainly God, our Maker, has the right, out of the same mass of human beings who by their own guilt have plunged themselves into the pit of misery, to elect some to everlasting life, and to allow others to remain in the abyss of wretchedness.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_potter_and.context: Hendriksen's section 3 of his Rom 9 outline is titled with the potter/clay catchword: 'Does not the potter have the right to make, out of the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?' He frames the section explicitly under 'God's Wrath and Mercy' and reads vv. 19-24 as defending the Creator's prerogative to elect and reprobate from a single fallen mass (infralapsarian framing).

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_free_will_.chapter: Chapter 9, Summary of Chapters 1-8 / Preview of Chapters 9-11
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_free_will_.quote_verbatim: The nation was rejected because of its unbelief (9:27, 31, 32; 10:21). ... But, as has been shown, for both Jew and Gentile the way of salvation is ever the same, namely, that of justification by faith, the product not of human works or merit but of divine sovereign grace.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_free_will_.context: Hendriksen holds together two claims: (1) Israel's rejection is genuinely 'because of its unbelief' — i.e. human unbelief is assigned as cause; (2) salvation itself is 'the product not of human works or merit but of divine sovereign grace.' He does not systematically resolve the resulting tension between sovereign election and the assignment of unbelief as cause of rejection; he simply states both.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_scope_of_s.chapter: Chapter 9 introduction (Summary of Chapters 1-8 and Preview of Chapters 9-11)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_scope_of_s.quote_verbatim: The Gentiles too are saved in no other way than by faith. This rule holds for everyone, without ethnic distinctions. (Rom 9:24-26; 10:4-13; 11:20, 23, 25). Paul shows how the disobedience of the Jews opens the door of salvation to the Gentiles, and how, in turn, the latter's salvation causes the Jews — in both cases the elect remnant, of course — to become filled with a jealousy that leads to salvation (11:11, 30, 31).
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_scope_of_s.context: Hendriksen explicitly frames salvation as ethnically undifferentiated and reciprocally provocative between Jew and Gentile, with the qualification 'in both cases the elect remnant' — i.e. universality of access does not collapse into universalism but operates through election.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.page: Rom 9:30-33 (conclusion of chapter 9) and chapter 9 introduction
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.quote_verbatim: The trouble with Israel was that these people proceeded from the false presupposition that by trying very, very hard they would be able, some day, to observe God's entire law, so that they would be able to shout, 'Success! We made it!' ... The law, with its uncompromising demand of perfect love and obedience, should have driven each Israelite to God with the fervent prayer, 'Oh, God, be thou merciful to me, the sinner.' Instead, Israel took for granted that men would be able, by their own power, and on the basis of their own resources, to fulfil the law's demands.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.context: Hendriksen treats Rom 9:30-32 as the climactic exposure of Jewish 'works'-righteousness. He insists 'there is no room whatever for boasting (3:27)' and that Israel's misconstrual was to read God's promises as 'conditioned on human merit and natural descent from Abraham, rather than on divine grace alone.'

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_paul_s_aut.chapter: Chapter 7, Sections 3b and 3c: Paul's own experience and that of others like him
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_paul_s_aut.quote_verbatim: What strikes us in reading Rom. 7:7-13 is the fact that, in discussing this subject of transgressing God's written law, Paul no less than ten times refers to himself. There are those who believe that Paul is here using the first person singular in a general sense, hence not in an autobiographical manner. Calvin did not share that view, and I believe Calvin was correct in taking that position. ... The reasons for believing that in 7:14-25 the regenerated individual, Paul, is describing his own condition and that of believers generally, have been given.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_paul_s_aut.context: Hendriksen against Kümmel/Ridderbos argues that Rom 7:7-25 is autobiographical, describing Paul's pre-conversion struggle (vv. 7-13) and Paul-the-believer's continuing struggle (vv. 14-25). He cites the 'change of tense' between v. 9a and v. 14ff and concludes 7:14-25 portrays Paul 'the believer, and by extension, the believer generally, including even the most mature.'

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_mora.chapter: Chapter 7, Section 3c: The wretched man's struggle and victory (7:14-25)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_mora.quote_verbatim: However, for the present, the Christian is living in an era in which two ages, the old and the new, overlap. There was a time when Paul was exclusively a sinner. There will be a time when he will be exclusively a saint. Right now, as he is dictating this letter, he is a sinner-saint. A 'saint,' to be sure; but also still a 'sinner'; hence the tension, the inner conflict. It is a struggle which every true believer experiences.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_mora.context: Hendriksen reads 7:14 ('I am carnal, sold as a slave to sin') as describing the regenerate Paul's continuing experience of moral inability vis-à-vis God's law. The believer experiences simultaneous bondage (to sin's presence) and freedom (through the Spirit's enabling). The argument node cites Rom 7:7 and 8:8; Hendriksen comments on both. On 8:8 (in his commentary on Rom 8, not included here verbatim) he repeats that 'those in the flesh cannot please God.'
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_mora.note_on_confidence: Medium because the argument also references Rom 8:7-8 commentary which lies in NTC vol. 12 chapter 8 (not in the supplied extracts). The Rom 7 portion of the claim is verbatim-supported; the 8:7-8 portion is supported by Hendriksen's own cross-reference but not directly extracted.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_the_role_o.quote_verbatim: Add to this the fact that the Jewish religious leaders had buried the original law of God under a load of oral traditions: minute, hair-splitting regulations touching just about every human activity and sphere of life. ... The law had become an unbearable yoke (Acts 15:10). Accordingly, what the apostle is now telling the membership of the Roman church is that from this yoke — in fact, even from Sinai's unadulterated written law regarded as a means whereby, through obedience, one can earn salvation — they have been released.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_the_role_o.context: Hendriksen distinguishes two functions of 'law': as expression of God's wise will (rule of gratitude for the believer) and as coercive code demanding obedience for salvation. The latter, especially when overlaid with rabbinic tradition, became an 'unbearable yoke' that 'stimulates sinful passions' (his comment on 7:5: 'sinful passions stimulated by the law'). True freedom is through death to the law in Christ's body, enabling 'service in newness of (the) Spirit.'

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_freedom_fr.page: Rom 7:1-6 and Practical Lessons on Verses 4 and 6
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_freedom_fr.chapter: Chapter 7, Section 3a: 'It produces the fruit of liberty: freedom from the law' (7:1-6)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_freedom_fr.quote_verbatim: It is clear from this that the genuine Christian life is not that of bondage but that of freedom. It is not motivated by external regulations but by love for the One to whom believers belong, even Christ. It is not guided by selfish interests but by the Spirit. And it is not barren but fruitful.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_freedom_fr.context: Hendriksen's exposition of 7:1-6 (especially 7:4 'made dead to the law through the body of Christ' and 7:6 'released from the law... we serve in newness of the Spirit') treats believers' release from law-as-coercive-code as the foundation of moral transformation. Liberty is not license: it 'produces fruit for God' through union with Christ and Spirit-empowered service.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.chapter: Chapter 5, Section C, 1a: 'It produces the fruit of peace and its concomitants' (5:1-11)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.quote_verbatim: Under the general heading Justification by Faith, Exposition (1:16-11:36) Paul has shown that this justification is necessary and real (1:16-3:31), as well as scriptural (chapter 4). In chapters 5-8 he demonstrates that it is also effective, fruitful. ... Here, in 5:1-11, the attention of the hearer and/or reader is focused first of all on peace. In connection with it mention is also made of freedom of access, exultation, and hope, a hope that is firmly anchored and amounts to certainty with respect to salvation.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_justificat.context: Hendriksen organizes Rom 5-8 as the demonstration that justification by faith is 'effective' (not merely forensic). The fruits enumerated for ch. 5 are: peace with God, access by faith, exultation in hope of glory, and firmly anchored hope. He explicitly contrasts the merely forensic-courtroom picture with God's fuller action: 'through his Spirit pours his love into his heart and adopts him as his own son or daughter.'

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_hope_as_an.quote_verbatim: Their hope is firmly anchored in God's redeeming love. Another way of expressing the same thought is this: their hope is moored to the throne of grace, that is, to that which is 'within the veil,' where Jesus is seated at God's right hand (Heb. 6:19, 20). He is living forevermore to intercede for his people (Heb. 7:25). ... Over against the opinion of some it should be emphasized that the expression 'the love of God' cannot mean 'our love for God.' How could such thoroughly inadequate love ever be the basis of hope that does not disappoint? The reference is clearly to God's own love, as verse 8 proves.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_hope_as_an.context: Hendriksen forcefully excludes the reading 'our love for God' for Rom 5:5 and grounds hope entirely in God's redeeming love poured out by the Holy Spirit, with the throne-of-grace / Christ's intercession imagery as the structural support.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_agen.quote_verbatim: Although it is true that perseverance (strength to bear up under plus the persistent application of this strength) is basically the result of the operation of the Holy Spirit in the hearts and lives of God's children, it implies human action. It is by no means a passive quality. The person who has it perseveres. He holds on to what he has (Rev. 2:25), is faithful even to the point of death (Rev. 2:10).
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_human_agen.context: Hendriksen states a cooperative model on Rom 5:3-4: divine grace is the basis of perseverance, but perseverance 'implies human action' and is 'by no means a passive quality'. He cross-applies this to reconciliation in 5:10: 'just as it is true that justification requires faith on man's part — God-imparted and God-sustained faith, to be sure, but human faith nevertheless — so also reconciliation requires obedience on man's part.'

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_creation_s.chapter: Chapter 8 (commentary not included in the supplied Romans 5/7/9 extracts)
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_creation_s.context: The argument describes Hendriksen's reading of Rom 8:20-22 ('Creation was subjected to futility not by its own choice'). His commentary on Rom 8 is in NTC vol. 12 (Baker, 1980) but is NOT contained in any of the three extract files at /04_Littérature_secondaire/08_Commentaires_NT/ (only Romans 5, 7 and 9 extracts are available locally). Hendriksen does refer forward to the believer's groaning in his discussion of 5:1-11 and 7:14-25, but the specific 'three groanings — creation, believers, Spirit' framing and the verbatim citation of 8:20 'not by its own choice' would need to be checked against NTC vol. 12 ch. 8 (not on disk).
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_creation_s.needs_followup: Locate NTC_Hendriksen_Romans 8.txt or print NTC vol. 12 pp. 254-269 (Hendriksen on Rom 8:18-25) to confirm verbatim wording.

scholarly_argument_hendriksen_believer_s.page: Rom 8:18-39 (NTC vol. 12 ad loc.); summary cross-ref in Rom 7:14-25 closing remarks
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_believer_s.chapter: Chapter 8 (full commentary not in supplied extracts) — partial cross-reference from chapter 7
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_believer_s.quote_verbatim: The cry he utters is one of distress, but not of despair, as verse 25 proves. Paul suffers agony, to be sure, the wretchedness brought about by strenuous exertion; that is, by trying hard, but never satisfactorily succeeding, to live in complete harmony with God's will but failing again and again. He is looking forward eagerly to the time when this struggle will have ended.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_believer_s.context: The argument's specific tripartite framing ('three groanings — creation, believers, Spirit — all pointing to eager expectation of future glory; ... more than conquerors (8:37)') is Hendriksen's reading of Rom 8:18-39. The Rom 7:24-25 passage above gives Hendriksen's adjacent treatment of believer-as-sinner-saint who 'is looking forward eagerly to the time when this struggle will have ended', but the full 8:22-37 commentary (vol. 12 ch. 8) is not in the on-disk extracts.
scholarly_argument_hendriksen_believer_s.needs_followup: Confirm against NTC vol. 12 ch. 8 (Rom 8:18-39) for the explicit 'three groanings' phrasing and the 8:28 / 8:37 citations.
